content: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) has been reported in case studies and series to produce significant clinical improvements in individuals with presumed viral myocarditis, leading to its widespread use in clinical practice. This review aimed to evaluate whether IVIG improves survival outcomes—both event-free survival (defined as survival without death, cardiac transplantation, or the need for a left ventricular assist device) and overall survival—in adults and children with presumed viral myocarditis compared to those who did not receive IVIG. Additionally, the review sought to identify specific patient subgroups who might derive the most benefit from IVIG based on factors such as age, symptom duration, symptom onset acuity, cardiac function at presentation, virological findings, or histological evidence of myocarditis. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, in July 2019, with additional searches in trial registries in November 2019. No language restrictions were applied. Studies were included if participants had a clinical diagnosis of acute myocarditis with specific cardiac function criteria (e.g., left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 0.45) and symptom duration of less than six months, and if they were randomly assigned to receive at least 1 g/kg of IVIG versus no IVIG or placebo. Studies were excluded if participants had received immunosuppressive therapy prior to outcome assessment or if myocarditis onset occurred within six months postpartum. Two reviewers independently screened the search results and extracted data. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool. Meta-analyses were conducted for two outcomes—overall survival and improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)—based on data from two adult trials. However, further meta-analyses were not feasible due to the limited number of trials and the heterogeneity of study populations and outcome measures. In this updated review, two new randomized trials were added to the two previously included trials. A quasi-randomized trial included in the earlier review was excluded in this update due to the availability of additional randomized evidence. For the two adult trials, the overall risk of bias was unclear, and the certainty of evidence for all outcomes was very low. The first adult trial involved 62 participants with recent-onset dilated cardiomyopathy who were randomly assigned to receive either IVIG or an equivalent volume of 0.1% albumin in a blinded manner. The effect of IVIG on event-free survival was uncertain, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.76 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48 to 6.40). The second adult trial included 41 participants with acute myocarditis who were randomized to receive high-dose IVIG (1–2 g/kg over two days) or no treatment. This trial reported longer survival times in the IVIG group after 60 days (P < 0.01), but no raw data were provided, and the evidence was deemed uncertain. When the number of deaths from both trials was pooled, no significant difference between groups was observed (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.23 to 3.62, I² = 31%, very low-certainty evidence). The effect of IVIG on LVEF after 12 months and at an unspecified time point was also uncertain (pooled mean difference [MD] −0.01, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.05). Functional capacity, assessed by peak oxygen consumption at 12 months, showed uncertain results (MD −0.80, 95% CI −4.57 to 2.97). Infusion-related side effects were reported with a very wide confidence interval, making the evidence highly uncertain (RR 20.29, 95% CI 1.25 to 329.93). Evidence regarding failure to achieve complete recovery was similarly uncertain (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.14). No data were reported on the effects of IVIG on left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVEDD), left ventricular shortening fraction (LVSF), or hospitalization status in adults. In the single pediatric trial included in the review, the overall risk of bias was low, but the certainty of evidence for all outcomes was very low. This trial involved 86 children in Egypt with acute myocarditis who were randomized to receive either 1 g/kg IVIG daily for two consecutive days or placebo. Echocardiographic assessments were performed at one and six months post-randomization to evaluate LVEDD and LVSF. The evidence for overall survival after six months was uncertain (RR for death 0.48, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.15). Similarly, the evidence for improvement in LVEDD and LVSF after six months was uncertain (LVEDD MD −4.00, 95% CI −9.52 to 1.52; no raw data for LVSF). No data were reported on the effects of IVIG on LVEF, functional capacity, side effects, complete recovery, or hospitalization status in children. In conclusion, the evidence from two adult trials with very low certainty and unclear risk of bias provides conflicting results regarding the use of IVIG in presumed viral myocarditis. One trial suggested that IVIG may prolong survival after 60 days, while the other found no significant benefit. In the single pediatric trial, the evidence for differences in survival, LVEDD, or LVSF was also of very low certainty. Until higher-quality studies with larger sample sizes and lower risk of bias are conducted, the efficacy of IVIG for presumed viral myocarditis remains uncertain. Further research into the pathophysiology of myocarditis is needed to improve diagnostic criteria and facilitate future studies.
